title: Principles of organisation; Animal tissues organs and organ systems

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metabolism
items.clue: The sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body.

items.label: tissue
items.clue: A group of cells with a similar structure and function.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: The part of an enzyme molecule that the substrate fits into.

items.label: Bile
items.clue: An alkaline liquid made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.stem: A structure in an organism is made up of several different tissues that work together to carry out a specific function. Which level of organisation is this structure?

options.text: a tissue, a group of similar cells
an organ system, a group of organs
an organ, an aggregation of tissues
an organism, a group of organ systems

questions.explanation: Correct: organs are aggregations of tissues performing specific functions, which is exactly what the structure described is.

questions.stem: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions. What causes this specificity?

options.text: The temperature at which the enzyme works.
The shape of the enzyme's active site.
The amount of the enzyme that is used.
The pH at which the enzyme is stored.

questions.explanation: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site, which only one substrate fits.

questions.stem: Which statement about organ systems in a living organism is correct?

options.text: Organ systems are made of one organ with one function.
Organ systems are made of cells grouped together.
Organ systems are made of one tissue with a function.
Organ systems are made of organs that work together.

questions.explanation: Correct: organs are organised into organ systems, which work together to form organisms.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the lock and key theory of enzyme action?

options.text: The enzyme fits into every kind of substrate.
The enzyme is used up by its own substrate.
The enzyme changes shape to fit any substrate.
The substrate fits the enzyme's active site.

questions.explanation: In the lock and key theory, used as a simplified model of enzyme action, the substrate is the key that fits the active site of the enzyme.

questions.stem: An enzyme-controlled reaction is fastest at 40 degrees Celsius. What happens at 60 degrees Celsius?

options.text: The rate falls because the enzyme has been killed.
The rate falls because the enzyme is used up.
The rate rises because the enzyme works faster.
The rate falls because the active site changes shape.

questions.explanation: Above the optimum temperature the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and the rate falls.

questions.stem: Protease in the stomach works fastest at pH 2. What happens to its activity at pH 8?

options.text: It falls, as the active site changes shape.
It rises, as enzymes work best at about pH 7.
It falls, as the enzyme is killed by alkali.
It falls, as the enzyme has been used up.

questions.explanation: Away from its optimum pH the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and activity falls.

questions.stem: Amylase broke down 20 mg of starch in 5 minutes. What was the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 4 mg per minute
0.25 mg per minute
20 mg per minute
100 mg per minute

questions.explanation: The mean rate is the amount changed divided by the time taken: 20 mg divided by 5 minutes.

questions.stem: Enzymes are involved in metabolism. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of metabolism in cells.
Enzymes give the reactions the energy that they need.
Enzymes are used up in the reactions that they speed up.
Enzymes catalyse only reactions that break down food.

questions.explanation: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, and each of those reactions is catalysed by an enzyme.

questions.stem: Which statement about digestive enzymes is correct?

options.text: Bile is the enzyme that breaks down fat droplets.
One enzyme is able to digest every type of food.
Protease is made in the stomach and pancreas.
Amylase is made only in the wall of the stomach.

questions.explanation: Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine, and it breaks down proteins to amino acids.

questions.stem: What does lipase break lipids down into?

options.text: Glucose and fatty acids
Glycerol and fatty acids
Amino acids and simple sugars
Small droplets of lipid

questions.explanation: Lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids, which are small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.

questions.stem: Why does bile increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase?

options.text: It digests the fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
It gives the lipase the energy that it needs.
It emulsifies fat, so surface area increases.
It makes the small intestine neutral at pH 7.

questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of breakdown by lipase.

questions.stem: What happens to the products of digestion after they are absorbed?

options.text: Every product is turned into glucose and stored.
They are all used in respiration to give energy.
They build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
They join back to form the first food molecules.

questions.explanation: The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.
